query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐temperature liquid metal environments relevant to chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, adding strong oxide-forming elements (e.g., Al) to ferritic/martensitic steels promotes the in situ formation of a continuous, dense alumina (Al2O3) film that passivates the metal surface, thereby both impeding oxygen ingress and reducing the dissolution of protective elements (e.g., Cr and Fe).
generation.material_initial_state: Ferritic/martensitic steels (such as 9Cr steels) prepared in identical microstructural conditions, with one set containing a significant Al addition (or processed via ODS methods with Al) and a baseline set without Al addition.
generation.intervention: Expose both steel variants to a liquid lead or lead‐bismuth eutectic environment at elevated temperatures (around 600 °C) under controlled low oxygen concentrations to simulate service conditions in nuclear and chemical processing environments.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under both static and dynamic exposure settings, at 600 °C for prolonged durations (e.g., up to 2000 hours), with oxygen contents maintained near 10^(-6) wt% in the coolant. The steels should have similar grain size and processing history except for the Al content.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an adherent, continuous, and dense Al2O3 surface oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: The strong oxygen affinity of Al accelerates the nucleation and growth of a stable Al2O3 film during initial oxidation. This dense film acts as a diffusion barrier that restricts further migration of oxygen into the matrix and minimizes the outward dissolution of key alloying elements, thereby enhancing corrosion resistance compared to steels that form less protective, porous or discontinuous oxide layers (e.g., Cr-rich but noncontinuous films).
generation.predicted_outcome: Steels with the Al addition will exhibit lower corrosion depths, a more uniform and stable oxide film (as verified by microscopy and compositional analysis), and reduced rates of Fe and Cr dissolution compared to the baseline steels lacking Al under identical test conditions.
generation.baseline: Steels without the additional Al, which typically form less protective oxidation products (such as discontinuous Fe- and Cr-rich films) that permit more aggressive dissolution in liquid lead environments.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis should hold in high-temperature corrosive environments such as liquid lead or LBE under controlled oxygen conditions and for steels with a ferritic/martensitic microstructure; its validity in other environments (e.g., high-temperature water or gaseous conditions) or for entirely different alloy systems is not asserted.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative effect of Al content on the kinetics and morphology of the protective oxide layer is not fully determined; potential synergistic or inhibitory interactions with other alloying elements (e.g., Si) and the influence of microstructural nuances (e.g., oxide-dispersion particles) also need further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of 9Cr-based steels with identical processing and microstructural features except for the deliberate addition of Al in one set. Subject both sets to an identical exposure in liquid lead or lead-bismuth eutectic at 600 °C under controlled, low oxygen conditions for 2000 hours. Periodically analyze the corrosion layer using SEM, TEM, and EPMA to assess oxide continuity and measure corrosion depth. Additionally, monitor the coolant for dissolved Fe and Cr content.
measurements: Oxide film morphology and continuity (using TEM/EPMA/XRD)
Rate of Fe and Cr dissolution (via chemical analysis of the coolant)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing steels do not show a statistically significant improvement in corrosion resistance (i.e., similar corrosion depths, oxide film quality, and dissolution rates as the non-Al steels) under the test conditions, then the hypothesis that Al-induced continuous Al2O3 formation is the governing mechanism for enhanced corrosion resistance would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Traditional steels will be severely corroded in a lead and/or LBE environment, especially when the temperature is higher than 500 °C. The high dissolution rate of the main elements of steel in liquid lead brings great hidden dangers to the safe service of the structure materials. One of the main approaches to fight lead corrosion is to form a protective layer on the surface of the materials by a reasonable control of the oxygen content in liquid lead []. For traditional steel, such as T91, Fe- and Cr-rich oxide layers will form during oxidation, but their structure is not dense enough to protect the matrix, especially at a high temperature. Forming a more stable and protective oxide layer on the surface of steel by optimizing the alloy design received more attention on the materials R&D of LFR in recent years. Al has a strong oxygen affinity; the standard Gibbs formation energy and required oxygen concentration of Al oxidation in lead is lower than those of the Fe, Cr, and Si elements, while the thermodynamic stability of the oxidation product Al2O3 is stronger. The corrosion behavior of T91, 9Cr ODS, and 9CrAl ODS in liquid Pb was tested and compared after exposure up to 2000 h at 600 °C. The main conclusions obtained are as follows: The surface color and luster of the different corrode materials were quite different. The color of T91 is abundant with a metallic luster due to the formation of complex oxidation products and attached lead. Most of the surface of 9Cr ODS is gray-white with a metallic luster due to the covered metallic lead. The color of the 9CrAl surface is quite uniform without metallic luster; The corrosion of 9Cr ODS is slightly heavier than that of T91 after corrosion for 1000 h. An oxide layer that grows outward is locally formed outside of T91, which plays a certain positive role in corrosion resistance, while the fine-grained structure of ODS steel promotes the accelerated dissolution of Fe and Cr, resulting in a lower rate of formation of oxidation products; The maximum corrosion depth of 9CrAl ODS is 51.8 μm after corrosion for 2000 h, which is much lower than that of 9Cr-ODS steel.
